passage:
Dear Jeevan Bhaiya,
You said I could ask you anything, so here goes.
At Rohan's birthday on Saturday, one of the guys kept trying to put his arm round a girl from our class. She kept moving away and said "stop" twice. He laughed and said she was "just shy". Everyone else laughed too. I didn't, but I didn't say anything either, and I've felt bad since.
Then on Monday we had the health session at school. The counsellor said something simple: if someone says no, or moves away, or goes quiet, that's a no. Not "shy". No. And a yes has to be free, not pushed.
I stayed after and asked her some questions about protection and infections that I was too embarrassed to ask anyone. She answered straight, without making me feel stupid, and gave me a leaflet.
Next time, I'm going to say, "Bro, she said stop." Is that enough?
Deepak

qa.q: How many times did the girl say "stop"?
qa.a: She said "stop" twice.

qa.q: What has Deepak felt since the birthday party?
qa.a: Deepak has felt guilty and uneasy about staying silent while the girl was pressured and others laughed.

qa.q: What could Deepak do if something like this happens again?
qa.a: Deepak could clearly say "she said stop", stand with the girl, and tell a trusted adult if the behaviour continues.

qa.q: How might the girl at the party have felt when everyone laughed?
qa.a: She likely felt uncomfortable, unsafe and alone, since her clear "stop" was brushed off as being shy.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning that a no must be respected and seeking accurate sexual health information from a trusted adult.

passage:
Dear Eshaan,
Since you moved to Pune, I've been thinking about the difference between being alone and being lonely.
Sunday mornings I sit on the terrace and sketch the pigeons for two hours. No one talks to me, and I love it. My head feels quiet. That's the good kind.
But weekday lunch is different. You used to sit with me. Now I eat under the stairs, pretending to read. I watch groups laugh and my chest aches. That's the other kind, and it's been three months.
I decided I don't want to wait for it to fix itself. Yesterday I went to the chess club. I lost every game, but a girl named Farah said I should come back Thursday. I'm going.
Also, call me on Saturday? I miss arguing with you about comics.
Minakshi

qa.q: Where does Minakshi eat lunch on weekdays now?
qa.a: Minakshi eats under the stairs, pretending to read.

qa.q: What does Minakshi feel while watching groups laugh at lunch?
qa.a: Minakshi feels lonely and sad, with an aching chest, which is different from the calm of sketching alone on Sunday.

qa.q: What steps is Minakshi taking to ease the loneliness?
qa.a: Going to the chess club, planning to return Thursday, and asking Eshaan to call on Saturday.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Eshaan would probably feel missed and glad to be trusted with the truth, and happy that Minakshi is making new friends.

grounding: Shows a teenager telling chosen, restful solitude apart from painful isolation and taking steps to connect.

passage:
"Yamini, you've skipped lunch all week."
"Not hungry, Sabina."
"You said that last week too. And you left the dance group. You loved dance."
Yamini picked at her sleeve. "I just feel… empty. Every day. I can't sleep, and then I can't get up. It's been like this since the holidays."
Sabina sat down beside her on the bench. "That sounds really heavy. Thank you for telling me."
"Don't make it a big thing."
"I care about you, so I think it is. Can we go to Ms D'Souza together? Right now? I'll stay with you."
Yamini hesitated, then nodded.
In the counsellor's room, Ms D'Souza listened to all of it. "You did the right thing coming in," she said. "Feeling this way for weeks is something we can get help for." She called Yamini's mother that afternoon, and they set up a meeting for the next day.

qa.q: When did Yamini say she had been feeling like this since?
qa.a: Since the holidays.

qa.q: What does Yamini asking Sabina not to make it a big thing suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests Yamini felt ashamed and worried about being a burden, even though she was really struggling.

qa.q: What did Sabina do well when she noticed the signs?
qa.a: Sabina noticed the changes over weeks, listened without judging, and went with Yamini to the counsellor the same day instead of keeping it secret.

qa.q: How does Ms D'Souza respond to Yamini?
qa.a: The counsellor listens fully, tells Yamini she did the right thing, and calls her mother that afternoon to set up support.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising a friend's lasting sadness and withdrawal and getting help from a counsellor the same day.

passage:
Tuesday, 1:20 a.m.
Can't sleep again. I got into bed at eleven like Mum asked, but my brain switched on like a light. Scrolled till 12:30, then finished the physics worksheet under the blanket.
This morning at 6:30 I felt drugged. Fell asleep in first period. Manoj, my brother, found it hilarious and did an impression of me snoring at breakfast. Not funny.
Biology Miss said teens' body clocks shift later, so we're not lazy, just out of sync with school. That actually made me feel better.
New plan: phone charges in the kitchen from ten. Worksheets done before dinner, not after. Dim lamp and a novel in bed. Sunday no sleeping till noon, because that apparently makes Monday worse.
Manoj says it won't last. We'll see.
Elizabeth

qa.q: Where will the phone charge from ten?
qa.a: The phone charges in the kitchen from ten.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel after hearing what Biology Miss said about body clocks?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt relieved and less guilty, understanding the late nights weren't just laziness.

qa.q: Which parts of Elizabeth's plan are most likely to help, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the phone out of the bedroom and finishing homework before dinner, because they remove the two things that kept Elizabeth up past midnight.

qa.q: How does Manoj see his sibling's sleep problem?
qa.a: Manoj treats it as a joke, doing a snoring impression and doubting the plan will last.

grounding: Shows a teenager understanding a shifted body clock and planning around late-night phone use and study load.

passage:
The party in Nour's backyard in Leeds was loud and warm, fairy lights strung across the fence. Abebe, sixteen, was by the snack table when an older boy held out a vape. "Go on. Mango flavour. Everyone's having one."
Abebe's heart thumped. A few people turned to watch.
He and Nour had joked about this exact moment on the bus last week, practising lines like a silly play.
"Nah, I'm good, mate," Abebe said, easy, and picked up a lemonade instead. "Got a football trial Saturday."
"One won't kill you."
"Still no." He turned back to Nour. "You said you'd show me that new song?"
The older boy shrugged and moved on. Nour grinned and bumped his shoulder. "Smooth. Just like we practised."

qa.q: What flavour did the older boy say the vape was?
qa.a: He said it was mango flavour.

qa.q: What was Abebe feeling when people turned to watch?
qa.a: Abebe felt nervous, his heart thumping, and under pressure with others watching.

qa.q: What helped Abebe refuse without a big scene?
qa.a: He had practised lines with Nour, kept his no short and friendly, gave a simple reason, and changed the subject.

qa.q: How does Nour feel about how Abebe handled it?
qa.a: Nour seems proud and pleased, grinning and bumping his shoulder because the practice worked.

grounding: Shows a teenager using rehearsed refusal to turn down a vape offered by a peer.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10. Written by Neelam Joshi.
Dolma met me today about choosing a stream. Her parents want science with biology so she can study medicine. Her results show she scores well in biology, but her strongest marks and her real excitement are in art and design. When she talks about sketching buildings, she sits up and speaks fast. When she talks about medicine, she looks at the floor.
We did an interest and aptitude activity. It pointed to architecture, which needs maths and physics as well as drawing.
Dolma was nervous: "Papa will be disappointed." I invited her parents in for a meeting next Friday. Her father came today to pick her up; I told him briefly and he agreed to come.
Next: at Friday's meeting, share both options and let Dolma explain in her own words.

qa.q: Which career did the activity point to?
qa.a: It pointed to architecture.

qa.q: What does Dolma looking at the floor when talking about medicine suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Dolma feels reluctant and unexcited about medicine, and maybe anxious about letting her parents down.

qa.q: How could the Friday meeting help Dolma and her family decide?
qa.a: If the counsellor lays out both paths and Dolma explains her interests herself, the family can weigh her strengths and their hopes together.

qa.q: How might Dolma's father see her choice after the meeting?
qa.a: He may start to see architecture as a serious path that still uses her maths and science, which could ease his worries.

grounding: Shows a teenager matching strengths and interests to a stream while respectfully including family expectations.

passage:
A week before the municipal elections last year, a message landed in our family group: a photo of a candidate with the words "He will close all government schools!" My uncle forwarded it to everyone. I'm Wasim, and I was sixteen and didn't know how to check anything.
My friend Arnab said, "Where's the source? A photo with words isn't news."
So we looked. We found the candidate's actual speech on a local news site. He'd said he wanted to merge two small schools, not close all of them. Big difference.
I showed my uncle. He grumbled, but he deleted the forward.
That made me curious, so I read how the ward councillor is chosen and what they actually control. Roads, water, drains, not national laws.
Next year, I can vote for the first time. I want to know what I'm voting for.

qa.q: What did the candidate actually say in his speech?
qa.a: He'd said he wanted to merge two small schools, not close all of them.

qa.q: What was Wasim's uncle feeling when shown the real speech?
qa.a: The uncle felt a bit annoyed and embarrassed, grumbling, but accepted the truth enough to delete the forward.

qa.q: How could someone check a political claim like this?
qa.a: Ask where the source is, find the original speech or a reliable news report, and compare the claim with what was actually said.

qa.q: Why might Arnab react differently to the forward than Wasim's uncle?
qa.a: Arnab questioned it right away because a photo with words isn't news, while the uncle trusted it and passed it on.

grounding: Shows a teenager checking a political claim against the source and learning how local government and voting work.
